# 06 — truss arm: axial force paths

**Reference only. Do not edit this file.** Fill in `force-results.csv` and
`reflection.md` in this same folder. For Step 3, also add a photo or PDF of
your Case 2B free-body diagrams / matrix setup (`case2B-working.pdf`,
`case2B-working.jpg`, or similar).

**This builds directly on the worked truss-force notes provided with this
lab.** Those notes work through **Case 1** and **Case 2A** symbolically.
Don't re-derive those two cases here unless you want the practice — use the
worked notes as your reference, substitute the nominal values below, and
record the requested check values. **Case 2B is yours to set up and solve.**

This pass is intentionally force-only. We are not calculating deflections
or stresses yet; the goal is to understand how a triangulated arm carries
motor thrust through axial tension and compression, and how changing the
orientation or number of truss cells changes the load path.

## What's new this time

So far, most of the arm calculations have treated the arm as a beam. Here
we use a different idealization: a **pin-jointed truss**. Every member is
assumed to carry only an axial force, so each member is either in tension
or compression. Bending and shear within an individual truss member are
ignored.

The key idea is joint equilibrium. At every free node,

```text
sum Fx = 0
sum Fy = 0
```

If the unknown member forces are collected in a vector `N`, the joint
equations can be assembled into a matrix system

```text
H N = f
```

where `H` contains the direction cosines of the members meeting at each
free joint. Use the same sign convention as the worked notes:

- **positive N = tension**
- **negative N = compression**

## Given nominal geometry and load

Use these values for the entire assignment:

- Upward motor thrust: **P = 250 gf**
- Truss depth: **h = 30 mm**
- Nominal two-cell arm length: **L_total = 120 mm**
- Therefore, for Cases 1, 2A, and 2B, each cell has horizontal length
  **L = 60 mm**

For a 60 mm by 30 mm cell,

```text
ell = sqrt(L^2 + h^2)
c   = L / ell
s   = h / ell
```

Keep forces in **gf** throughout this pass. No conversion to N is needed.

## Case definitions

### Case 1 — single triangular cell

Case 1 is the first worked example from the notes. The loaded node is `A`,
and the two root nodes `B` and `C` are fixed to the body:

```text
B o-----------o A
             /   ^
          /      | P
       /
C o
```

Members: `AB`, `AC`.

For this numerical check, use `L = 60 mm`, `h = 30 mm`, and `P = 250 gf`.

### Case 2A — two cells, diagonal EB

Case 2A is the second worked example from the notes:

```text
D o-----------o B-----------o A
          /     |         /   ^
       /        |      /      | P
    /           |   /         |
E o-----------o C
```

Members: `AB`, `AC`, `BC`, `BD`, `CE`, `BE`.

Nodes `D` and `E` are fixed. The total arm length is 120 mm, so each cell is
60 mm long.

### Case 2B — two cells, diagonal DC

Case 2B changes only the diagonal in the left-hand cell:

```text
D o-----------o B-----------o A
    \           |         /   ^
       \        |      /      | P
          \     |   /         |
E o-----------o C
```

Members: `AB`, `AC`, `BC`, `BD`, `CE`, `DC`.

This is the case you will set up and solve yourself.

## Step 3 — Solve Case 2B

Do this one yourself.

1. Draw free-body diagrams of free joints `A`, `B`, and `C`. Assume each
   unknown member force is initially tensile (pointing away from the
   joint).
2. Write the two equilibrium equations at each joint.
3. Assemble the six equations into a matrix system of the same form used
   in the worked Case-2A example.
4. Solve for all six member forces.
5. Save a photo or PDF of your free-body diagrams / matrix setup in this
   folder as `case2B-working.pdf`, `case2B-working.jpg`, or similar.
6. Enter only the following numerical checks in `force-results.csv`:
   - `N_BC`
   - the force in the most highly loaded member, including its sign
   - `max_abs_N`

One of these values deserves special attention. Don't discard a result
just because it is zero or nearly zero — think about why joint equilibrium
permits that to happen for this particular load case.

## Step 4 — Compare Cases 2A and 2B

Use your complete numerical solutions to compare the two diagonal
arrangements.

First compare

```text
max |N_e|
```

for the two structures. Then look at the **sign** of the force in the member
where that maximum occurs.

Fill in the Case-2 comparison prompts in `reflection.md`.

The sign matters physically. A slender truss member loaded in compression
can fail by buckling even when the material stress is below its tensile or
yield strength. You do not need to calculate Euler buckling in this pass,
but you should recognize that equal force magnitude does not necessarily
mean equal structural risk.

## Step 5 — Add more cells without changing the arm size

Now keep the overall dimensions fixed:

```text
L_total = 120 mm
h       = 30 mm
P       = 250 gf
```

and subdivide the same arm into more cells. For `n` cells,

```text
cell width = L_total / n
```

Use top nodes

```text
T0, T1, ..., Tn
```

and bottom nodes

```text
B0, B1, ..., B(n-1)
```

with `T0` and `B0` fixed to the body and the upward thrust applied at `Tn`.
There is **no bottom node underneath the motor node `Tn`**. Therefore the
rightmost cell remains a triangle, exactly as in Cases 1, 2A, and 2B.

For example, a four-cell arm has the topology

```text
T0 o-------o-------o-------o-------o T4
         / |     / |     / |     /
      /    |  /    |  /    |  /
B0 o-------o-------o-------o
```

The last bottom node is `B3`; there is no `B4`, no lower horizontal member
under the motor, and no vertical member at the motor location.

For every `n`, include:

- `n` top-chord members
- `n-1` bottom-chord members
- `n-1` vertical members
- `n` diagonal members

so the truss remains statically determinate.

Analyze **n = 3, 4, and 6** for each of the following two diagonal families.
Case 2A and Case 2B are the corresponding `n = 2` baselines.

### Family A — same orientation as Case 2A

In every complete rectangular cell, the diagonal runs from the
**bottom-left node to the top-right node**. The final motor-side triangle
also runs from its lower-left node to the motor node.

For four cells:

```text
T0 o-------o-------o-------o-------o T4
         / |     / |     / |     /
      /    |  /    |  /    |  /
B0 o-------o-------o-------o
```

### Family B — same orientation as Case 2B

In every complete rectangular cell, the diagonal runs from the
**top-left node to the bottom-right node**. The final motor-side triangle
still runs from the last bottom node upward to the motor node, exactly as
in Case 2B.

For four cells:

```text
T0 o-------o-------o-------o-------o T4
    \       |\       |\       |     /
       \    |   \    |   \    |  /
B0 o-------o-------o-------o
```

You should examine the full member-force solution for `n = 3, 4, 6`, but
do **not** enter a separate set of numbers for every case. In
`force-results.csv`, report only the `n = 6` endpoint values for each
family:

- the magnitude of a diagonal-member force, `diag_abs_N`
- the overall maximum member-force magnitude, `max_abs_N`

Use your calculations for the intermediate values to answer the trend
questions in `reflection.md`.
